notes.meaning: God told Moses to go speak to Pharaoh again. Even though God had hardened Pharaoh's heart and the hearts of his officials, this was done so God could display His miraculous power. These signs showed both Egypt and Israel that the Lord is the one true ruler of the world.

differ.view: God's hardening is a sovereign and unconditional choice to hand an already stubborn sinner over to his own rebellion.
God gave Pharaoh over to his own stubbornness only after Pharaoh repeatedly refused God's calls to repent.
God creates no new evil in a person, but hardens a sinner simply by holding back His grace.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: God did not destroy Pharaoh's free will, but permitted Pharaoh's heart to grow hard as he resisted God's works.

notes.meaning: God commanded that these mighty wonders be remembered and passed down through the family. Parents and grandparents were to tell their children how God brought judgment on Egypt. Hearing these stories helps each new generation place their trust in the Lord.

Moses and Aaron confronted Pharaoh with a direct question from the Lord. They asked how long he would refuse to humble himself and let God's people go to worship. True humility before God means obeying His commands in daily action, not just saying sorry when trouble comes.

Moses warned Pharaoh that a plague of locusts would arrive the very next day if he refused to obey. Giving an exact time showed that this swarm was sent by God and was not a random accident of nature. These locusts were large grasshoppers that could destroy all remaining plant life in their path.

The swarm of locusts would be so thick that the ground itself could not be seen. They would eat up every plant and tree that had survived the earlier hail storm. This would strip Egypt bare and leave the land facing famine.

The locusts would force their way into the royal palace, the homes of the court officials, and every Egyptian house. A swarm of this size had never been seen by any earlier generation in Egypt's history. After delivering this stern warning, Moses turned and walked out of Pharaoh's presence.

Pharaoh's own officials urged him to give in to Moses. They asked how long Moses would be a trap bringing disaster on them, and they pointed out that Egypt was already in ruins. Even these royal advisers could see that continuing to fight against God was useless.

Moses and Aaron were brought back into the palace before the plague could strike. Pharaoh told them they could go worship the Lord, but he asked who would be going. He wanted to work out a compromise so he would not lose complete control over his slaves.

Moses insisted that the whole nation must leave together. The young and the old, sons and daughters, and all their herds had to go celebrate a feast to the Lord. God calls the entire family to take part in worship together.

Pharaoh angrily rejected the plan and cursed them, saying the Lord would have to be with them if he ever let their children go. He claimed the Israelites had evil plans to run away for good. By keeping the children behind as hostages, Pharaoh hoped to force the parents to return.

differ.view: Satan works like Pharaoh to keep young children from serving God early in their lives.

notes.meaning: Pharaoh told Moses that only the adult men could go, falsely claiming that this was all they had ever asked. He then had Moses and Aaron chased out of his court by force. Proud leaders often become angry when they realize they cannot force God's servants to compromise.

The Lord commanded Moses to stretch his hand out over Egypt so the locusts would come. The insects were ordered to devour all the plants that survived the hail. Moses acted with God's authority over the created world.

Moses raised his staff, and God sent an east wind that blew across the land all day and night. By morning, the wind carried a vast cloud of locusts into Egypt from the Arabian desert. God often directs the wind and weather to carry out His divine plans.

The locusts spread out and settled across every region of Egypt. There had never been such a massive swarm before, and there would never be another one like it. The vast size of the swarm showed that it was brought by God's direct hand.

The insects covered the land until the ground looked black, and they devoured every green leaf and fruit left on the trees. Nothing green remained anywhere in Egypt. This demonstrated that Egypt's false gods, who were supposed to protect crops and bring life, were completely powerless before the Lord.

Pharaoh hurriedly sent messengers to bring Moses and Aaron back to the palace. He openly admitted that he had sinned against the Lord and against them. Terrible disasters can make even hardened leaders speak words of confession.

Pharaoh asked Moses to forgive him this one time and pray for God to take away this deadly plague. He called the locusts a death because they brought total starvation to the country. Sadly, he only wanted relief from the pain of his punishment, not a changed heart.

Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to the Lord to remove the swarm. He interceded for the king to show God's great patience and to continue God's work of deliverance. God graciously listens to the prayers of His servants.

God answered Moses by shifting the wind into a powerful west wind. The strong gusts swept up all the locusts and drowned them in the Red Sea until not one remained in Egypt. God proved that He has full power to take away a judgment just as easily as He brings it.

Even after the land was cleared of locusts, the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart. The king went back on his word and refused to let the Israelites leave. Pharaoh's continued rebellion prepared the way for God's final judgments.

The Lord told Moses to stretch his hand toward heaven to bring a heavy darkness over Egypt. This ninth plague came without any warning because Pharaoh had broken his promise. The darkness was so thick and clammy that people could physically feel its heavy gloom.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest God used a severe desert sandstorm, called a khamsin, to blot out the sun with thick dust.

notes.meaning: Moses lifted his hand toward the sky, and pitch-black darkness covered all of Egypt for three days. The sun vanished, leaving the whole nation trapped in total shadow. This proved that Amon-Re, Egypt's chief sun god, was entirely helpless before the true Lord of heaven.

The darkness was so complete that people could not see one another, and nobody left their home for three days. Heavy vapors likely put out their lamps and fires. Yet the Israelites had light in their homes, showing God's loving protection over His own people.

Pharaoh summoned Moses and agreed that all the Israelites, including the children, could go worship the Lord. However, he insisted that their sheep, goats, and cattle stay behind in Egypt. He hoped that keeping their property would force them to return to slavery.

differ.view: Pharaoh represents worldly rulers who try to convince believers to leave their treasure and property in the world.

notes.meaning: Moses refused to accept Pharaoh's conditions. He pointed out that they needed their livestock to present sacrifices and offerings to God. Worshiping God means giving Him what He asks for without holding anything back.

Moses told the king that every animal must go, and not a single hoof would be left behind. They could not know what sacrifices God would require until they arrived at the place of worship. Believers must follow God with complete obedience rather than accepting human compromises.

The Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart once again, and he refused to let the people go. Instead of yielding to God's clear authority, Pharaoh chose stubborn anger. His hard heart led his kingdom toward complete ruin.

Pharaoh lost his temper and ordered Moses to leave his presence forever. He threatened Moses with death if he ever tried to see his face again. When proud people reject God's truth, they often turn their anger against God's messenger.

Moses answered that Pharaoh had spoken the truth, and they would never see each other's face again. Moses knew that God's final judgment was coming and that Israel's freedom was now certain. When people drive God's word away, the time for patient warning has come to an end.
